claim: A prerequisite for the systems biology analysis of tissues is an accurate digital three-dimensional reconstruction of tissue structure based on images of markers covering multiple scales.
source: A prerequisite for the systems biology analysis of tissues is an accurate digital three-dimensional reconstruction of tissue structure based on images of markers covering multiple scales.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that establishes a foundational requirement for systems biology analysis of tissues.

claim: The pipeline includes newly developed algorithms that address specific challenges of thick dense tissue reconstruction.
source: Our pipeline includes newly developed algorithms that address specific challenges of thick dense tissue reconstruction.
evidence: The authors explicitly state that their pipeline contains novel algorithms designed for specific reconstruction challenges.

claim: The implementation allows for a flexible workflow, scalable to high-throughput analysis and applicable to various mammalian tissues.
source: Our implementation allows for a flexible workflow, scalable to high-throughput analysis and applicable to various mammalian tissues.
evidence: The authors describe the capabilities of their implementation in terms of flexibility, scalability, and applicability.

claim: The pipeline was applied to the analysis of liver tissue and extracted quantitative parameters of sinusoids, bile canaliculi and cell shapes.
source: We applied it to the analysis of liver tissue and extracted quantitative parameters of sinusoids, bile canaliculi and cell shapes, recognizing different liver cell types with high accuracy.
evidence: The authors state they applied their method to liver tissue and obtained specific quantitative measurements.

claim: The pipeline recognizes different liver cell types with high accuracy.
source: We applied it to the analysis of liver tissue and extracted quantitative parameters of sinusoids, bile canaliculi and cell shapes, recognizing different liver cell types with high accuracy.
evidence: The authors explicitly claim high accuracy in cell type recognition.

claim: The platform uncovered an unexpected zonation pattern of hepatocytes with different size, nuclei and DNA content.
source: Using our platform, we uncovered an unexpected zonation pattern of hepatocytes with different size, nuclei and DNA content, thus revealing new features of liver tissue organization.
evidence: The authors explicitly state they discovered a previously unknown zonation pattern in hepatocytes.

claim: The pipeline proved effective to analyse lung and kidney tissue, demonstrating its generality and robustness.
source: The pipeline also proved effective to analyse lung and kidney tissue, demonstrating its generality and robustness.
evidence: The authors explicitly state they tested the pipeline on lung and kidney tissues with successful results.

claim: A major challenge for understanding mammalian tissue structure and function is the ability to monitor cellular processes across different levels of complexity, from the subcellular to the tissue scale.
source: A major challenge for the understanding of mammalian tissue structure and function is the ability to monitor cellular processes across different levels of complexity, from the subcellular to the tissue scale (Megason and Fraser, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work establishing this as a known challenge in the field.

claim: Quantitative functional models can be used to describe and predict system behaviour under perturbed conditions.
source: This information can then be used to develop quantitative functional models that describe and predict the system behaviour under perturbed conditions (Hunter et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2011; Fonseca et al., 2011; Sbalzarini, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work on quantitative modeling.

claim: The development of multi-scale models requires first a geometrical model of the tissue, that is, an accurate three-dimensional (3D) digital representation of the cells in the tissue as well as their critical subcellular components.
source: The development of such multi-scale models requires first a geometrical model of the tissue, that is, an accurate three-dimensional (3D) digital representation of the cells in the tissue as well as their critical subcellular components (Peng et al., 2010; Boehm et al., 2010; Mayer et al., 2012).
evidence: This requirement is stated explicitly and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Organelles can be as small as ~0.1 µm in size.
source: Since organelles can be as small as ~0.1 µm in size, the geometrical model has also to cover a wide range of scales spanning over three orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is a factual statement about organelle size that establishes the scale requirements for imaging.

claim: Substantial limitations persist with respect to availability of markers, volume of tissue to reconstruct, scale of measurements, computational methods to perform the analysis and sample throughput.
source: However, substantial limitations persist with respect to availability of markers, volume of tissue to reconstruct, scale of measurements, computational methods to perform the analysis and sample throughput.
evidence: The authors identify multiple existing limitations in the field.

claim: A few existing platforms provide standard tools for 3D segmentation and methods to process 2D surface layers of cells.
source: Although a few existing platforms provide standard tools for 3D segmentation and methods to process 2D surface layers of cells [ImageJ/Fiji (Girish and Vijayalakshmi, 2004; Collins, 2007), ICY (de Chaumont et al., 2012) and MorphoGraphX (Barbier de Reuille et al., 2015)], the challenges posed by dense and thick tissue specimens require the development of new algorithms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to existing software platforms.

claim: The challenges posed by dense and thick tissue specimens require the development of new algorithms.
source: Although a few existing platforms provide standard tools for 3D segmentation and methods to process 2D surface layers of cells [ImageJ/Fiji (Girish and Vijayalakshmi, 2004; Collins, 2007), ICY (de Chaumont et al., 2012) and MorphoGraphX (Barbier de Reuille et al., 2015)], the challenges posed by dense and thick tissue specimens require the development of new algorithms.
evidence: The authors argue that existing tools are insufficient for dense tissue analysis.

claim: There is a demand for a platform that can provide the required set of methods for the reconstruction of multi-scale digital 3D geometrical models of mammalian tissues from confocal microscopy images.
source: Therefore, there is a demand for a platform that can provide the required set of methods for the reconstruction of multi-scale digital 3D geometrical models of mammalian tissues from confocal microscopy images.
evidence: The authors identify an unmet need in the field that their work addresses.

claim: The number of fluorescent markers that can be used simultaneously is limited to 4–5.
source: The number of fluorescent markers that can be used simultaneously is limited to 4–5, making the reconstruction of tissue models a challenging problem.
evidence: This is a technical limitation stated as fact based on current imaging technology.

claim: For a meaningful model, it is necessary to properly identify the different cell types within the tissue but also to detect subcellular and extracellular structures.
source: For a meaningful model, it is necessary to properly identify the different cell types within the tissue but also to detect subcellular and extracellular structures, for example, nuclei, plasma membrane or cell cortex, extracellular matrix (ECM) and cell polarity.
evidence: The authors state requirements for creating meaningful tissue models.

claim: Automated morphological cell recognition is a possible way to reconstruct dense tissue with limited number of markers.
source: Automated morphological cell recognition is a possible way to reconstruct dense tissue with limited number of markers.
evidence: The authors propose automated morphological recognition as a solution to marker limitations.

claim: Validated fluorescent protein chimeras are not always available, especially in the appropriate combination of fluorescence emission spectral profiles.
source: Validated fluorescent protein chimeras are not always available, especially in the appropriate combination of fluorescence emission spectral profiles.
evidence: This is a statement about practical limitations in available fluorescent markers.

claim: In dense tissues immunostaining is inhomogeneous due to restricted antibody penetration.
source: On the other hand, in dense tissues immunostaining is inhomogeneous due to restricted antibody penetration.
evidence: This is a known technical challenge in tissue staining.

claim: The development of protocols that render tissues optically transparent and permeable to macromolecules without significantly compromising their general structure enables the imaging of relatively thick specimens.
source: The development of protocols that render tissues optically transparent and permeable to macromolecules without significantly compromising their general structure enables the imaging of relatively thick specimens (Chung and Deisseroth, 2013; Ke et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to tissue clearing methods.

claim: In the case of a densely packed tissue, for example, liver, homogeneous staining is still limited to a thickness of ~100 µm.
source: However, in the case of a densely packed tissue, for example, liver, homogeneous staining is still limited to a thickness of ~100 µm.
evidence: This is a specific technical limitation observed for liver tissue staining.

claim: Obtaining high-resolution data from large volumes of tissue requires sectioning the sample into serial 100-µm-thick slices that are stained and imaged separately.
source: Therefore, obtaining high-resolution data from large volumes of tissue (typically from 0.1 mm to a few centimetres) requires sectioning the sample into serial 100-µm-thick slices that are stained and imaged separately.
evidence: The authors describe their approach to imaging large tissue volumes.

claim: The cutting process introduces artefacts, such as bending, uneven section surfaces and partial damage of tissue, that require corrections during tissue model reconstruction.
source: Furthermore, the cutting process introduces artefacts, such as bending, uneven section surfaces and partial damage of tissue, that require corrections during tissue model reconstruction.
evidence: The authors identify specific artifacts introduced by tissue sectioning.

claim: The publicly available generic image processing software is unable to deal with such problems.
source: Unfortunately, the publicly available generic image processing software is unable to deal with such problems.
evidence: The authors state that existing software cannot handle the artifacts from tissue sectioning.

claim: The authors developed a set of new algorithms as well as implementing established ones in an adjustable pipeline implemented in stand-alone freely available software.
source: In this study, we addressed these challenges by developing a set of new algorithms as well as implementing established ones in an adjustable pipeline implemented in stand-alone freely available software (http://motiontracking.mpi-cbg.de).
evidence: The authors describe their contribution as both novel algorithms and implementation of existing methods.

claim: The authors tested the pipeline on the reconstruction of a geometrical model of liver tissue as proof of principle.
source: As proof of principle, we tested the pipeline on the reconstruction of a geometrical model of liver tissue.
evidence: The authors explicitly state they used liver tissue as a test case.

claim: The authors created a benchmark for the evaluation of dense tissue reconstruction algorithms comprising a set of realistic 3D images generated from the digital model of liver tissue.
source: In order to test the accuracy of the pipeline, we created a benchmark for the evaluation of dense tissue reconstruction algorithms comprising a set of realistic 3D images generated from the digital model of liver tissue.
evidence: The authors describe creating a benchmark dataset for validation.

claim: Only a few geometrical models of liver tissue have been published.
source: Despite its importance and a long history of histological studies, only a few geometrical models of liver tissue have been published (Hardman et al., 2007; Hoehme et al., 2010; Hammad et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the limited existing literature on liver tissue models.

claim: The liver is composed of functional units, the lobules.
source: The liver is composed of functional units, the lobules.
evidence: This is a basic anatomical fact about liver structure.

claim: In each lobule, bile canaliculi and sinusoidal endothelial cells form two 3D networks between the portal vein (PV) and the central vein (CV).
source: In each lobule, bile canaliculi and sinusoidal endothelial cells form two 3D networks between the portal vein (PV) and the central vein (CV).
evidence: This describes the anatomical organization of liver lobules.

claim: The bile canalicular (BC) network is formed by hepatocytes and transports the bile.
source: The bile canalicular (BC) network is formed by hepatocytes and transports the bile, whereas the sinusoidal endothelial network transports the blood.
evidence: This describes the function and cellular composition of the BC network.

claim: The sinusoidal endothelial network transports the blood.
source: The bile canalicular (BC) network is formed by hepatocytes and transports the bile, whereas the sinusoidal endothelial network transports the blood.
evidence: This describes the function of the sinusoidal network.

claim: One remarkable feature of liver tissue is the zonation of metabolic functions due to the fact that the hepatocytes located in the vicinity of the PV do not have the same metabolic activities as the hepatocytes located near the CV.
source: One is the zonation of metabolic functions due to the fact that the hepatocytes located in the vicinity of the PV do not have the same metabolic activities as the hepatocytes located near the CV (Kuntz and Kuntz, 2006).
evidence: This claim about metabolic zonation is supported by a citation.

claim: Hepatocytes are remarkably heterogeneous in terms of number of nuclei (mono- and bi-nucleated) and ploidy.
source: Second, hepatocytes are remarkably heterogeneous in terms of number of nuclei (mono- and bi-nucleated) and ploidy (Martin et al., 2002; Guidotti et al., 2003; Faggioli et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim about hepatocyte heterogeneity is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The lobules contain two additional important cell types, stellate and Kupffer cells.
source: Third, the lobules contain two additional important cell types, stellate and Kupffer cells (Baratta et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim about liver cell types is supported by a citation.

claim: The authors established a workflow for confocal imaging of mouse liver specimens.
source: To analyse the 3D organization of liver tissue, we established a workflow for confocal imaging of mouse liver specimens and developed an adjustable pipeline of new and established image analysis algorithms to process the images and build digital models of the tissue (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The authors describe establishing an imaging workflow.

claim: The authors established a protocol for the preparation of tissue specimens for single- and double-photon confocal microscopy at different resolutions.
source: First, we established a protocol for the preparation of tissue specimens for single- and double-photon confocal microscopy at different resolutions.
evidence: The authors describe developing a tissue preparation protocol.

claim: To cover multiple scales from subcellular organelles to tissue spanning over three orders of magnitude, the authors used a 3D multi-resolution tissue image acquisition approach.
source: To cover multiple scales from subcellular organelles to tissue spanning over three orders of magnitude, we used a 3D multi-resolution tissue image acquisition approach (Figure 1A).
evidence: The authors describe their multi-resolution imaging strategy, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The multi-resolution imaging consisted of imaging a tissue sample at low resolution (1 μm × 1 μm × 1 μm per voxel) and zooming on the parts of interest at high resolution (0.3 μm × 0.3 μm × 0.3 μm per voxel).
source: This consisted of imaging a tissue sample at low resolution (1 μm × 1 μm × 1 μm per voxel) and zooming on the parts of interest at high resolution (0.3 μm × 0.3 μm × 0.3 μm per voxel).
evidence: The authors provide specific resolution parameters for their imaging approach.

claim: Mouse livers were fixed by trans-cardial perfusion instead of the conventional immersion fixation to minimize the time lag between the termination of blood flow and fixation.
source: Mouse livers were fixed by trans-cardial perfusion instead of the conventional immersion fixation (Burton et al., 1987) to minimize the time lag between the termination of blood flow and fixation (Gage et al., 2012).
evidence: The authors describe their fixation method with citations supporting the rationale.

claim: Trans-cardial perfusion fixation proved to be absolutely essential to preserve the tissue architecture and the epitopes for immunostaining.
source: This proved to be absolutely essential to preserve the tissue architecture and the epitopes for immunostaining.
evidence: The authors state the importance of their fixation method based on their observations.

claim: Serial sections of fixed tissues were prepared at a thickness of 100 µm to maximize antibody penetration and limit laser light scattering.
source: Serial sections of fixed tissues were prepared at a thickness of 100 µm to maximize antibody penetration and limit laser light scattering.
evidence: The authors explain their choice of section thickness with specific rationale.

claim: Liver sections were stained to visualize key subcellular and tissue structures, namely nuclei (DAPI), the apical surfaces of hepatocytes (CD13), the sinusoidal endothelial cells (Flk1) or ECM (Laminin and Fibronectin) and the cell cortex (F-actin stained by phalloidin).
source: Liver sections were stained to visualize key subcellular and tissue structures, namely nuclei (DAPI), the apical surfaces of hepatocytes (CD13), the sinusoidal endothelial cells (Flk1) or ECM (Laminin and Fibronectin) and the cell cortex (F-actin stained by phalloidin).
evidence: The authors describe the specific markers used for staining different tissue structures.

claim: The authors tested various reagents and protocols to clear the liver tissue, such as glycerol and 2,2′thiodiethanol (TDE), and found that SeeDB yielded the best results.
source: We tested various reagents and protocols to clear the liver tissue, such as glycerol and 2,2′thiodiethanol (TDE), and found that SeeDB (Ke et al., 2013) yielded the best results.
evidence: The authors describe testing different clearing methods and identifying the best one.

claim: Stained sections were imaged sequentially (generating Z-stacks) by one- and two-photon laser scanning confocal microscopy to maximize the number of fluorescent channels available.
source: Stained sections were imaged sequentially (generating Z-stacks) by one- and two-photon laser scanning confocal microscopy to maximize the number of fluorescent channels available.
evidence: The authors describe their imaging strategy to overcome channel limitations.

claim: The same section was imaged twice, at low and high magnification, using 25×/0.8 and 63×/1.3 objectives, respectively.
source: The same section was imaged twice, at low and high magnification, using 25×/0.8 and 63×/1.3 objectives, respectively.
evidence: The authors provide specific details about the objectives used for multi-resolution imaging.

claim: The registration of 3D high-resolution images within low-resolution ones provides tissue-scale context information that is essential for the interpretation of the data at the cellular and subcellular level.
source: The registration of 3D high-resolution images within low-resolution ones provides tissue-scale context information that is essential for the interpretation of the data at the cellular and subcellular level.
evidence: The authors explain the importance of their multi-resolution registration approach.

claim: A major problem for the image analysis of thick tissue sections is the low signal-to-noise ratio deep into the tissue, especially for stainings that yield high and diffuse background.
source: A major problem for the image analysis of thick tissue sections is the low signal-to-noise ratio deep into the tissue, especially for stainings that yield high and diffuse background (e.g. actin staining with phalloidin throughout the cytoplasm).
evidence: The authors identify a specific technical challenge in thick tissue imaging.

claim: The authors developed a new Bayesian de-noising algorithm that first makes a probabilistic estimation of the background and separates it from the foreground.
source: To address this problem, we developed a new Bayesian de-noising algorithm that first makes a probabilistic estimation of the background and separates it from the foreground (see 'Methods').
evidence: The authors describe developing a novel denoising algorithm.

claim: BFBD de-noising provides better results than the standard ones in the field, such as median filtering, Gauss low-pass filtering and anisotropic diffusion.
source: BFBD de-noising provides better results than the standard ones in the field, such as median filtering, Gauss low-pass filtering and anisotropic diffusion (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), but also outperforms (by quality and computational performance) other algorithms, known to be more elaborate, such as the 'Pure Denoise' (Luisier et al., 2010) and 'edge preserving de-noising and smoothing' (Beck and Teboulle, 2009) (see 'Methods') (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The authors compare their method to existing methods with references to figures showing the comparison.

claim: The partially overlapping (~10% overlap) low-resolution images of each physical section were combined in 3D mosaics using the normalized cross-correlation (NCC) approach.
source: In more detail, the partially overlapping (~10% overlap) low-resolution images of each physical section were combined in 3D mosaics (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) using the normalized cross-correlation (NCC) approach (see 'Methods').
evidence: The authors describe their image stitching method with reference to figures.

claim: NCC was chosen because it allows finding accurate shifts given a coarse initial match between 3D images.
source: NCC was chosen because it allows finding accurate shifts given a coarse initial match between 3D images (Emmenlauer et al., 2009; Peng et al., 2010; Bria and Iannello, 2012).
evidence: The authors explain their choice of method with citations to supporting literature.

claim: The mechanical distortion and tissue damage produced by sectioning are such that even advanced and well-established methods for image stitching fail due to the lack of texture correlations between adjacent sections.
source: The mechanical distortion and tissue damage produced by sectioning are such (as illustrated in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) that even advanced and well-established methods for image stitching (Preibisch et al., 2009; Saalfeld et al., 2012; Hayworth et al., 2015) fail due to the lack of texture correlations between adjacent sections.
evidence: The authors identify limitations of existing methods with citations and figure references.

claim: The authors developed a Bayesian algorithm for stitching images of bended and partially damaged soft tissue sections.
source: To address this problem, we developed a Bayesian algorithm for stitching images of bended and partially damaged soft tissue sections.
evidence: The authors describe developing a novel algorithm to address a specific problem.

claim: The Bayesian stitching algorithm first corrects section bending and then uses the empty space at the interior of large structures (e.g. vessels) within adjacent sections to register and stitch them.
source: The algorithm first corrects section bending and then uses the empty space at the interior of large structures (e.g. vessels) within adjacent sections to register and stitch them.
evidence: The authors describe the steps of their novel algorithm.

claim: The surface predicted by the algorithm closely matched the surface detected manually.
source: The surface predicted by the algorithm closely matched the surface detected manually (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The authors validate their algorithm by comparison to manual detection, with reference to a figure.

claim: The authors first segmented the large vessels and then aligned the sections by matching them.
source: Therefore, we first segmented the large vessels and then aligned the sections by matching them (Figure 2D).
evidence: The authors describe their approach to section alignment with figure reference.

claim: The vessels were segmented by using the local maximum entropy (LME) approach.
source: The vessels were segmented by using the local maximum entropy (LME) approach (Brink, 1996) (see 'Methods').
evidence: The authors describe their vessel segmentation method with citation.

claim: The segmented vessels were classified (marked as PV or CV) revealing the precise arrangement of lobule-level structures.
source: Subsequently, the segmented vessels were classified (marked as PV or CV) revealing the precise arrangement of lobule-level structures.
evidence: The authors describe classifying vessels to understand tissue organization.

claim: The authors interpolated vessels within the gaps caused by tissue removal by tri-linear intensity approximation.
source: Finally, we interpolated these vessels within the gaps caused by tissue removal by tri-linear intensity approximation.
evidence: The authors describe their method for handling gaps in tissue sections.

claim: The authors registered the high-resolution images within the low-resolution model using rigid body transformation.
source: Following the assembly of the low-resolution model, we registered the high-resolution images within it using rigid body transformation.
evidence: The authors describe their registration method.

claim: To accelerate the search for registration parameters, the authors built a hierarchy of binned images and performed registration sequentially from the coarsest to the finest one.
source: To accelerate the search for registration parameters, we built a hierarchy of binned images and performed registration sequentially from the coarsest to the finest one (see 'Methods').
evidence: The authors describe an optimization strategy for registration.

claim: The reconstruction covers about 1300 μm × 1300 μm × 600 μm of the tissue.
source: The reconstruction covers about 1300 μm × 1300 μm × 600 μm of the tissue and is presented in Figure 2E and Video 1.
evidence: The authors provide specific dimensions of their reconstructed tissue volume with figure and video references.

claim: Global thresholding approaches may produce segmentation artefacts in 3D confocal images that are usually heterogeneous in intensity due to staining unevenness and light scattering in the tissue.
source: However, since 3D confocal images are usually heterogeneous in intensity due to staining unevenness and light scattering in the tissue (Lee and Bajcsy, 2006), global thresholding approaches may produce segmentation artefacts.
evidence: The authors identify a limitation of global thresholding with citation.

claim: Local thresholding allows adjusting the segmentation threshold to the spatial variability.
source: In contrast, local thresholding allows adjusting the segmentation threshold to the spatial variability.
evidence: The authors explain the advantage of local thresholding.

claim: The authors applied the LME method to find segmentation thresholds in the de-noised images.
source: We applied the LME method to find segmentation thresholds in the de-noised images.
evidence: The authors describe applying a specific method for segmentation.

claim: The LME segmentation approach produced two major artefacts: the objects were moderately swollen and contained holes resulting from local uneven staining.
source: However, this segmentation approach produced two major artefacts. The objects were moderately swollen and contained holes resulting from local uneven staining.
evidence: The authors identify specific artifacts from their initial segmentation approach.

claim: Standard approaches to close the holes by morphological operations (opening/closing) led to even higher overestimation of the diameter of thin structures, such as sinusoids and BC.
source: We used standard approaches to close the holes by morphological operations (opening/closing), which unfortunately led to even higher overestimation of the diameter of thin structures, such as sinusoids and BC.
evidence: The authors identify a problem with standard morphological operations.

claim: The authors extended the segmentation algorithm by generating a triangulation mesh of the segmented surfaces by the cube marching algorithm and tuning the active mesh so that the triangle mesh vertexes aligned to the maximum gradient of fluorescence intensity in the original image.
source: We generated a triangulation mesh of the segmented surfaces by the cube marching algorithm (Lorensen and Cline, 1987) (Figure 3A). Then, we tuned the active mesh so that the triangle mesh vertexes aligned to the maximum gradient of fluorescence intensity in the original image (Figure 3A).
evidence: The authors describe their improved segmentation approach with citation and figure reference.

claim: The authors generated a representation of the skeletonized image via a 3D graph describing the geometrical and topological features of the BC and sinusoidal networks.
source: Finally, we generated a representation of the skeletonized image via a 3D graph describing the geometrical and topological features of the BC and sinusoidal networks.
evidence: The authors describe creating a graph representation of tubular networks.

claim: Closely packed nuclei are optically not well-resolved in 3D confocal images, resulting in artificially merged structures.
source: However, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B, closely packed nuclei are optically not well-resolved in 3D confocal images, resulting in artificially merged structures.
evidence: The authors identify a specific imaging challenge with figure reference.

claim: 30–60% (depending on the animal strain and age) of hepatocytes in adult liver are bi-nucleated.
source: Since 30–60% (depending on the animal strain and age) of hepatocytes in adult liver are bi-nucleated, artificial nuclei merging compromises the tissue analysis.
evidence: The authors provide a specific statistic about hepatocyte bi-nucleation.

claim: The authors used a probabilistic algorithm for double- and multi-nuclei splitting.
source: To address this problem, we used a probabilistic algorithm for double- and multi-nuclei splitting (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The authors describe their approach to splitting merged nuclei with figure reference.

claim: The nuclei splitting algorithm achieved an accuracy of over 90% when tested in both synthetic and real 3D images.
source: Tested in both synthetic and real 3D images, the algorithm proved capable of splitting clustered nuclei with different degrees of overlap (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K) with an accuracy of over 90%.
evidence: The authors provide quantitative validation of their algorithm with figure reference.

claim: The nuclei splitting approach achieved similar accuracy values to other recently published voxel-based methods for nuclei segmentation.
source: Although this approach is based on active triangulation mesh, it achieved similar accuracy values to other recently published voxel-based methods for nuclei segmentation (Amat et al., 2014; Chittajallu et al., 2015).
evidence: The authors compare their method's performance to published methods with citations.

claim: A previous automated classification system discriminated hepatocytes from non-parenchymal cells in 2D human liver images with a 97.8% accuracy.
source: A previous automated classification system discriminated hepatocytes from non-parenchymal cells in 2D human liver images with a 97.8% accuracy (O'Gorman et al., 1985).
evidence: The authors cite previous work on cell classification for comparison.

claim: The automatic classification of non-parenchymal cells in 3D liver tissue is more challenging.
source: However, the automatic classification of non-parenchymal cells in 3D liver tissue is more challenging.
evidence: The authors state that 3D classification is more difficult than 2D.

claim: The authors designed an algorithm to automatically classify different cell types in the tissue based on nuclear morphological features.
source: Given their importance in physiology and disease (Bouwens et al., 1992; Kmiec, 2001; Malik et al., 2002) and the limitation on the number of fluorescent markers that can be simultaneously imaged, we designed an algorithm to automatically classify different cell types in the tissue based on nuclear morphological features.
evidence: The authors describe developing a classification algorithm with citations supporting the importance of the problem.

claim: The authors chose two deterministic supervised classifiers, linear discriminant analysis (LDA) and Bayesian network classifier (BNC).
source: We chose two deterministic supervised classifiers, linear discriminant analysis (LDA) and Bayesian network classifier (BNC).
evidence: The authors describe their choice of classification methods.

claim: LDA is a fundamental and widely used technique to classify data into several mutually exclusive groups.
source: LDA, also known as Fisher LDA (Fisher, 1936), is a fundamental and widely used technique to classify data into several mutually exclusive groups (Duda et al., 2001).
evidence: The authors describe LDA with citations to foundational work.

claim: LDA has been successfully applied for nuclei discrimination in microscopy images.
source: It has been successfully applied for nuclei discrimination in microscopy images (Huisman et al., 2007; Lin et al., 2007).
evidence: The authors cite previous applications of LDA to similar problems.

claim: BNCs show good performance and allow for probabilistic classification.
source: On the other hand, BNCs are more recently developed classifiers which not only show good performance but also allow for probabilistic classification.
evidence: The authors describe advantages of BNCs.

claim: BNCs reveal the hierarchy of parameters used for the classification.
source: In addition, BNCs reveal the hierarchy of parameters used for the classification (Friedman et al., 1997), which may provide insights into underlying biological processes.
evidence: The authors describe an additional advantage of BNCs with citation.

claim: The authors manually built a training set of 2301 nuclei using specific cellular markers.
source: As input for the classifiers, we manually built a training set of 2301 nuclei using specific cellular markers (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) and computed for each nucleus a profile of 74 parameters (Table 1) describing nuclei morphology, texture and localization relative to sinusoids and cell borders (density of actin in vicinity of nuclei) (see 'Methods').
evidence: The authors describe creating a training dataset with figure and table references.

claim: Both LDA and BNC classifiers recognized hepatocytes with ~100% accuracy.
source: Both classifiers recognized hepatocytes with ~100% accuracy, thus further improving the previous performance (O'Gorman et al., 1985).
evidence: The authors report classification performance with comparison to previous work.

claim: The overall cell-type classification yielded 95.4% and 92.6% accuracy for the LDA and BNC, respectively.
source: The overall cell-type classification yielded 95.4% and 92.6% accuracy for the LDA and BNC, respectively.
evidence: The authors report overall classification accuracy for both methods.

claim: The classification algorithms achieved accuracy higher than 90% for discriminating non-parenchymal cells.
source: Although discriminating non-parenchymal cells is difficult even for a person skilled in the art, our algorithms achieved accuracy higher than 90%.
evidence: The authors report high accuracy for a challenging classification task.

claim: The first largest population of cells corresponds to hepatocytes (44.6% ± 2.7%, mean ± SEM) followed by sinusoidal endothelial cells (29.8% ± 2.5%).
source: As expected, the first largest population of cells corresponds to hepatocytes (44.6% ± 2.7%, mean ± SEM) followed by sinusoidal endothelial cells (29.8% ± 2.5%).
evidence: The authors report quantitative cell population statistics.

claim: The percentage of Kupffer cells (8.7% ± 0.7%) was lower than that of stellate cells (11.2% ± 1.0%), against previous estimates on 2D images.
source: Surprisingly, we found important quantitative differences for Kupffer and stellate cells. The percentage of Kupffer cells (8.7% ± 0.7%) was lower than that of stellate cells (11.2% ± 1.0%), against previous estimates on 2D images (Baratta et al., 2009).
evidence: The authors report unexpected findings that differ from previous literature with citation.

claim: The percentage of other cells was 5.7% ± 0.8%.
source: The percentage of other cells was 5.7% ± 0.8%.
evidence: The authors report the percentage of unclassified cells.

claim: Cells were segmented by expansion of the active mesh from the nuclei to the cell surface.
source: Finally, cells were segmented by expansion of the active mesh from the nuclei to the cell surface.
evidence: The authors describe their cell segmentation method.

claim: The active mesh expansion algorithm over-segmented bi-nucleated cells into two cells with a single nucleus.
source: However, this algorithm over-segmented bi-nucleated cells into two cells with a single nucleus.
evidence: The authors identify a limitation of their initial cell segmentation approach.

claim: The authors used phalloidin intensity and nucleus-to-nucleus distance to recognize over segmented multinuclear cells and merge them.
source: Therefore, we used phalloidin intensity and nucleus-to-nucleus distance to recognize over segmented multinuclear cells and merge them.
evidence: The authors describe their solution to the over-segmentation problem.

claim: A manual check of segmentation of 2559 cells revealed only ~2% error for hepatocyte segmentation.
source: A manual check of segmentation of 2559 cells revealed only ~2% error for hepatocyte segmentation that is a further improvement of the state-of-the-art achievements by voxel-based segmentation methods (Mosaliganti et al., 2012).
evidence: The authors report validation results with comparison to existing methods.

claim: The authors generated a set of artificial images of liver tissue that can be used for developing and evaluating methods for the reconstruction of geometrical models of dense tissue.
source: We generated a set of artificial images of liver tissue that can be used for developing and evaluating methods for the reconstruction of geometrical models of dense tissue.
evidence: The authors describe creating a benchmark dataset.

claim: The benchmark consists of a set of realistic 3D high-resolution images (0.3 μm × 0.3 μm × 0.3 μm per voxel) of normal liver tissue.
source: The benchmark consists of a set of realistic 3D high-resolution images (0.3 μm × 0.3 μm × 0.3 μm per voxel) of normal liver tissue.
evidence: The authors describe the specifications of their benchmark dataset.

claim: The benchmark images and models are provided as supplementary material.
source: Given their general usefulness for testing image analysis software, the benchmark images and models are provided as supplementary material (Supplementary file 1, Morales-Navarrete et al., 2016).
evidence: The authors state they are making their benchmark publicly available.

claim: For tubular structures, the authors achieved average F-scores of 0.90 ± 0.04 and 0.73 ± 0.06 for sinusoidal and BC networks, respectively.
source: For tubular structures, we achieved average (over the different noise level sets) F-scores of 0.90 ± 0.04 and 0.73 ± 0.06 for sinusoidal and BC networks, respectively.
evidence: The authors report quantitative validation results for tubular network reconstruction.

claim: For nuclei and cell segmentation, the authors found average F-scores 0.91 ± 0.03 and 0.92 ± 0.03, respectively.
source: In the case of the nuclei and cell segmentation, we found average F-scores 0.91 ± 0.03 and 0.92 ± 0.03, respectively.
evidence: The authors report quantitative validation results for nuclei and cell segmentation.

claim: The authors obtained values of 2.72 ± 0.13 µm (ground truth value = 3.0 µm) and 0.58 ± 0.05 µm (ground truth value = 0.5 µm) for sinusoidal and BC networks radius, respectively.
source: We obtained values of 2.72 ± 0.13 µm (ground truth value = 3.0 µm) and 0.58 ± 0.05 µm (ground truth value = 0.5 µm) for sinusoidal and BC networks, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 7M,N).
evidence: The authors report accuracy of morphometric measurements with figure reference.

claim: The average error for cell volume estimation was found to be 5.17% ± 1.97%.
source: The average error for cell volume estimation was found to be 5.17% ± 1.97% (Figure 3—figure supplement 7O).
evidence: The authors report cell volume estimation accuracy with figure reference.

claim: The benchmark experiments showed high accuracy for the reconstruction of the 'ground truth' models of all the morphologically different structures forming the liver tissue.
source: The benchmark experiments showed high accuracy for the reconstruction of the 'ground truth' models of all the morphologically different structures forming the liver tissue (Figure 3—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The authors summarize their validation results with figure reference.

claim: The authors applied their software to quantitatively analyse the geometric features of liver tissue from three adult mice.
source: Next, we applied our software to quantitatively analyse the geometric features of liver tissue from three adult mice.
evidence: The authors describe applying their method to real biological samples.

claim: A critical parameter for blood flux models is the radius of sinusoids.
source: A critical parameter for blood flux models is the radius of sinusoids.
evidence: The authors identify an important parameter for modeling.

claim: The authors measured a radius of 4.0 ± 1.1 μm for sinusoids, a value close to quantifications by electron microscopy (EM) analysis.
source: We measured a radius of 4.0 ± 1.1 μm, a value close to quantifications by electron microscopy (EM) analysis (Wisse et al., 1985; Oda et al., 2003; McCuskey, 2008).
evidence: The authors report a measurement and compare it to literature values with citations.

claim: In the sinusoidal networks, the authors determined the angles between two branching arms to be 111.6° ± 12.37°, against previous estimates.
source: In the sinusoidal networks, we determined the angles between two branching arms to be 111.6° ± 12.37° (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), against previous estimates (Hammad et al., 2014).
evidence: The authors report a measurement that differs from previous literature with citation and figure reference.

claim: The values for the BC network branching angles are similar to the sinusoidal network (110.36° ± 9.85°).
source: Moreover, the values for the BC network are similar to the sinusoidal network (110.36° ± 9.85°, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The authors report a measurement for BC network with figure reference.

claim: Recent studies on the morphometric parameters of the liver tissue provided either average values or limited data measurements of the hepatocytes volume, omitting information on their heterogeneity.
source: Recent studies on the morphometric parameters of the liver tissue (Hammad et al., 2014; Friebel et al., 2015) provided either average values or limited data measurements of the hepatocytes volume, omitting information on their heterogeneity.
evidence: The authors identify limitations in previous studies with citations.

claim: The authors found a multi-modal distribution of hepatocyte volumes in line with measurements on isolated hepatocytes.
source: Interestingly, we found a multi-modal distribution of hepatocyte volumes (Figure 4A) in line with measurements on isolated hepatocytes (Martin et al., 2002).
evidence: The authors report a finding consistent with previous work with citation and figure reference.

claim: The distribution of volumes of both mono- and bi-nucleated hepatocytes can be independently described by a mixture of two populations.
source: The distribution of volumes of both mono- and bi-nucleated hepatocytes can be independently described by a mixture of two populations with mean volumes 3126 ± 1302 µm3 (~14% of cells) and 5313 ± 1175 µm3 (~10% of cells), and 5678 ± 1176 µm3 (~45% of cells) and 10606 ± 1532 µm3 (~30% of cells), respectively (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The authors report detailed statistical analysis of cell volumes with figure reference.

claim: A population of mono-nucleated hepatocytes can have a volume that does not differ from that of bi-nucleated hepatocytes.
source: Hence, surprisingly, although the bi-nucleated hepatocytes are assumed to be larger than the mono-nucleated, we found that a population of mono-nucleated hepatocytes can have a volume that does not differ from that of bi-nucleated hepatocytes (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: The authors report a surprising finding with figure reference.

claim: The resulting distribution of DAPI integral intensity shows three well-separated peaks.
source: The resulting distribution (Figure 4D) shows three well-separated peaks.
evidence: The authors describe a distribution pattern with figure reference.

claim: The three peaks in DAPI integral intensity distribution presumably correspond to the 2n (diploid nuclei), 4n and 8n (polyploid nuclei) DNA content previously reported.
source: These presumably correspond to the 2n (diploid nuclei), 4n and 8n (polyploid nuclei) DNA content previously reported (Guidotti et al., 2003; Martin et al., 2002) (note that this analysis does not resolve the aneuploidy of specific chromosomes (Faggioli et al., 2011)).
evidence: The authors interpret their findings in the context of previous literature with citations.

claim: In the small bi-nucleated hepatocytes (volume < 8000 µm3) both nuclei had 2n DNA content, whereas in the large hepatocytes (volume > 8000 µm3) both had 4n DNA content.
source: Interestingly, in the small bi-nucleated hepatocytes (volume < 8000 µm3) both nuclei had 2n DNA content, whereas in the large hepatocytes (volume > 8000 µm3) both had 4n DNA content.
evidence: The authors report a specific relationship between cell size and DNA content.

claim: Almost no bi-nuclear hepatocytes (<1.0%) with different amount of DNA per nucleus were observed.
source: Almost no bi-nuclear hepatocytes (<1.0%) with different amount of DNA per nucleus (e.g. one nucleus with 2n and one with 4n) were observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: The authors report a quantitative observation with figure reference.

claim: The hepatocyte volume does not depend on the number of nuclei but rather on their polyploidy, in agreement with previous reports.
source: These results suggest that the hepatocyte volume does not depend on the number of nuclei but rather on their polyploidy, in agreement with previous reports (Miyaoka and Miyajima, 2013).
evidence: The authors draw a conclusion supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The authors identified seven populations of hepatocytes: 2n, 4n, 8n, 16n for mono-nuclear and 2×2n, 2×4n, 2×8n for bi-nuclear hepatocytes.
source: Therefore, we classified hepatocytes with respect to number of nuclei, volume and DNA content using a hierarchical cluster algorithm. We identified seven populations, namely 2n, 4n, 8n, 16n for mono-nuclear and 2×2n, 2×4n, 2×8n for bi-nuclear hepatocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E,F).
evidence: The authors report classification results with figure reference.

claim: Four populations (mono-nucleated 2n and 4n, and bi-nucleated 2×2n and 2×4n) were major, representing around 97% of all hepatocytes.
source: Four populations (mono-nucleated 2n and 4n, and bi-nucleated 2×2n and 2×4n) were major, representing around 97% of all hepatocytes.
evidence: The authors report the relative abundance of different hepatocyte populations.

claim: The reports on the spatial distribution of polyploid hepatocytes are controversial.
source: The reports on the spatial distribution of polyploid hepatocytes are controversial (Gentric and Desdouets, 2014).
evidence: The authors identify controversy in the literature with citation.

claim: Some studies suggest that periportal hepatocytes show a lower polyploidy than the perivenous ones.
source: Whereas some suggest that periportal hepatocytes show a lower polyploidy than the perivenous ones (Gandillet et al., 2003; Asahina et al., 2006), others suggest that both regions have similar polyploid compositions (Margall-Ducos et al., 2007; Pandit et al., 2012).
evidence: The authors cite conflicting reports in the literature.

claim: The authors found a pronounced zonation in the localization of mono- and bi-nucleated hepatocytes within the lobule.
source: Strikingly, we found a pronounced zonation in their localization.
evidence: The authors report a striking finding about spatial organization.

claim: The 2n mono-nucleated hepatocytes were enriched in the PC and PV regions.
source: Whereas the 2n mono-nucleated were enriched in the PC and PV regions, mono-nucleated 4n showed a homogeneous distribution between PV and PC regions (Figure 5).
evidence: The authors report spatial distribution patterns with figure reference.

claim: Mono-nucleated 4n hepatocytes showed a homogeneous distribution between PV and PC regions.
source: Whereas the 2n mono-nucleated were enriched in the PC and PV regions, mono-nucleated 4n showed a homogeneous distribution between PV and PC regions (Figure 5).
evidence: The authors report spatial distribution patterns with figure reference.

claim: The 2×2n bi-nucleated hepatocytes have a similar pattern as the 2n mono-nucleated (highly enriched in the CV and PV regions).
source: The 2×2n bi-nucleated hepatocytes have a similar pattern as the 2n mono-nucleated (highly enriched in the CV and PV regions), but the density of 2×4n bi-nucleated was lower in those regions and increased in the middle region (Figure 5).
evidence: The authors report spatial distribution patterns with figure reference.

claim: The density of 2×4n bi-nucleated hepatocytes was lower in CV and PV regions and increased in the middle region.
source: The 2×2n bi-nucleated hepatocytes have a similar pattern as the 2n mono-nucleated (highly enriched in the CV and PV regions), but the density of 2×4n bi-nucleated was lower in those regions and increased in the middle region (Figure 5).
evidence: The authors report spatial distribution patterns with figure reference.

claim: This is the first time that polyploidy and poly-nuclearity are found to be zonated and follow a specific pattern.
source: As far as we know, this is the first time that polyploidy and poly-nuclearity are found to be zonated and follow a specific pattern.
evidence: The authors claim novelty of their finding.

claim: These findings have important implications for both the structural organization of liver tissue and its proliferating and metabolic activities.
source: These findings have important implications for both the structural organization of liver tissue and its proliferating and metabolic activities.
evidence: The authors discuss the significance of their findings.

claim: The pipeline allowed generating geometrical reconstructions of lung and kidney tissues without fine-tuning of the parameters.
source: The pipeline allowed us to generate geometrical reconstructions of the tissues (Figure 6 and Videos 4 and 5, respectively) without fine-tuning of the parameters.
evidence: The authors demonstrate the generalizability of their method with figure and video references.

claim: In the lung, alveolar cells constitute around 19% of the volume, consistent with previous measurements.
source: For example, in the lung, we found that the alveolar cells constitute around 19% of the volume, consistent with previous measurements (Irvin and Bates, 2003).
evidence: The authors report a measurement consistent with literature with citation.

claim: In the kidney, proximal tubule cells have larger volumes than distal tubule cells, in agreement with previous studies.
source: In the kidney, we found that proximal tubule cells have larger volumes than distal tubule cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), also in agreement with previous studies (Nyengaard et al., 1993; Rasch and Dørup, 1997).
evidence: The authors report a measurement consistent with literature with citations and figure reference.

claim: The pipeline is versatile and able to reconstruct geometrical models of tissues with fairly different architectures.
source: Altogether, the new data show that our pipeline is versatile and able to reconstruct geometrical models of tissues with fairly different architectures.
evidence: The authors conclude about the versatility of their method based on the data.

claim: The platform developed overcomes critical bottlenecks such as lack of automation, limited accuracy and low throughput analysis.
source: The platform developed here overcomes such bottlenecks in that it (1) achieves high accuracy of geometric reconstruction, (2) can process large volumes of imaged tissue, for example, a full liver lobule, (3) increases the image analysis performance to such an extent that the model reconstruction time is shorter than the biological experimental time and compatible with middle-throughput (this is achieved by combining the computational efficiency of C++ with the CPU/GPU multi-threading capabilities), (4) can be run on a regular PC and (5) provides a flexible tool for constructing image processing pipelines that are tuneable for specific tissue and imaging conditions.
evidence: The authors list specific advantages of their platform.

claim: The newly developed algorithms both increase the quality of the results and deal with problems for which there appears currently to be no real good solutions available.
source: The newly developed algorithms both increase the quality of the results (e.g. 3D image de-noising, LME method, active mesh tuning, cell classification) and deal with problems for which there appears currently to be no real good solutions available (e.g. correction of tissue deformation and combination of individual sections in the case of partial tissue removal) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The authors summarize the contributions of their novel algorithms with figure reference.

claim: The platform is implemented as stand-alone free to download software.
source: Our platform is implemented as stand-alone free to download software (http://motiontracking.mpi-cbg.de).
evidence: The authors state the availability of their software.

claim: The authors created a benchmark of realistic images (with the underlying ground truth model) for the evaluation of 3D segmentation algorithms in biological images.
source: Furthermore, we created a benchmark of realistic images (with the underlying ground truth model) for the evaluation of 3D segmentation algorithms in biological images (Supplementary file 1, Morales-Navarrete et al., 2016).
evidence: The authors describe creating a resource for the community.

claim: The analysis revealed an unexpected zonation pattern of hepatocytes with different size, nuclei and DNA content within the liver lobule.
source: Our analysis revealed an unexpected zonation pattern of hepatocytes with different size, nuclei and DNA content within the liver lobule.
evidence: The authors summarize a key biological finding.

claim: A major limiting factor in the development of a comprehensive geometrical model is the trade-off between imaging large volumes of samples to gain a view of the overall tissue architecture and imaging at high-resolution to achieve an accurate description of the structures at the limit of resolution of the light microscope.
source: A major limiting factor in the development of a comprehensive geometrical model is the trade-off between imaging large volumes of samples to gain a view of the overall tissue architecture and imaging at high-resolution to achieve an accurate description of the structures at the limit of resolution of the light microscope, for example, the apical surface of hepatocytes forming the BC network.
evidence: The authors identify a fundamental challenge in tissue imaging.

claim: The measured morphological features and parameters are embedded in their proper context of tissue architecture.
source: In this way, the measured morphological features (e.g. BC) and parameters (e.g. cell size) are embedded in their proper context of tissue architecture.
evidence: The authors explain the advantage of their multi-resolution approach.

claim: The hepatocyte volume is a parameter that has little value as average without considering the distribution of parameter values in the lobule.
source: For example, the hepatocyte volume is a parameter that has little value as average without considering the distribution of parameter values in the lobule (Figure 5).
evidence: The authors argue for the importance of spatial context with figure reference.

claim: The diversity of geometric features of the cells within the liver lobule could provide new insights into the regulation of metabolic zonation.
source: In general, the diversity of geometric features of the cells within the liver lobule could provide new insights into the regulation of metabolic zonation (see below).
evidence: The authors suggest potential implications of their findings.

claim: The nuclei reconstruction approach achieved accuracy higher than 90%.
source: Our nuclei reconstruction approach achieved accuracy higher than 90%.
evidence: The authors report the performance of their nuclei reconstruction method.

claim: The major source of errors in nuclei reconstruction is over-segmented nuclei.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1K, the major source of errors is over-segmented nuclei.
evidence: The authors identify the main type of error in their method with figure reference.

claim: In a few cases (~2%), binuclear cells were mistaken for two separate cells due to weak staining of the cell cortex.
source: Even though our cell segmentation method proved able to identify and reconstruct cells with high accuracy, in a few cases (~2%), binuclear cells were mistaken for two separate cells due to weak staining of the cell cortex.
evidence: The authors identify a specific limitation of their cell segmentation method.

claim: The active mesh tuning allowed improving the accuracy of segmentation of the BC and sinusoidal networks.
source: The active mesh tuning allowed improving the accuracy of segmentation of the BC and sinusoidal networks.
evidence: The authors state the benefit of their active mesh tuning approach.

claim: The accuracy of a geometrical model is indispensable for the development of predictive models of tissue function.
source: This is important since the accuracy of a geometrical model is indispensable for the development of predictive models of tissue function.
evidence: The authors explain the importance of accuracy for modeling.

claim: The geometrical model yielded a diameter of the sinusoidal-walled tube equal to the typical size of erythrocytes and lymphocytes.
source: Our geometrical model yielded a diameter of the sinusoidal-walled tube equal to the typical size of erythrocytes and lymphocytes.
evidence: The authors report a measurement from their model.

claim: The geometrical model supports the model of active exchange of blood serum and lymph in the space of Disse, whereby blood flux propels cells through the sinusoids causing waves of capillary walls deformation.
source: Therefore, it supports the model of active exchange of blood serum and lymph in the space of Disse, whereby blood flux propels cells through the sinusoids causing waves of capillary walls deformation (McCuskey, 2008; Wisse et al., 1985).
evidence: The authors interpret their findings in the context of existing models with citations.

claim: The active mesh tuning algorithm yielded a distribution of the radius of sinusoid capillaries with a mean value that was 20% lower than previously estimated by similar approaches, but in line with the values reported by EM.
source: The active mesh tuning algorithm yielded a distribution of the radius of sinusoid capillaries with a mean value that was 20% lower (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) than previously estimated by similar approaches (Hammad et al., 2014; Hoehme et al., 2010), but in line with the values reported by EM (Wisse et al., 1985).
evidence: The authors compare their measurements to previous work with citations and figure reference.

claim: The reconstruction revealed a large difference with the previously reported angles between two arms of branching sinusoids (112° vs. 32°).
source: The reconstruction also revealed a large difference with the previously reported angles between two arms of branching sinusoids (112° vs. 32°, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The authors report a measurement that differs significantly from previous literature with figure reference.

claim: The geometrical model provides correct values for other sinusoidal network parameters such as number of intersection nodes per mm3 (8.3 × 104 ± 1.9 × 104) and network length per mm3 (3.1 × 106 ± 0.3 × 106 µm), which appear to have been overestimated in a recent report.
source: Moreover, the geometrical model provides correct values for other sinusoidal network parameters such as number of intersection nodes per mm3 (8.3 × 104 ± 1.9 × 104) and network length per mm3 (3.1 × 106 ± 0.3 × 106 µm), which appear to have been overestimated in a recent report (Hammad et al., 2014) (see 'Methods').
evidence: The authors report measurements and suggest previous work overestimated these values with citation.

claim: The discrepancy between the authors' geometrical model and others could be due to differences in image processing and/or experimental procedures.
source: The discrepancy between our geometrical model and others (Hoehme et al., 2010; Hammad et al., 2014) could be due to differences in image processing and/or experimental procedures (tissue fixation, image acquisition, etc.).
evidence: The authors speculate on reasons for differences with previous work with citations.

claim: The platform's active mesh approach may yield a more precise geometrical reconstruction in comparison with voxel-based methods.
source: One possible explanation for this discrepancy is that our platform applies the active mesh approach to the segmentation of structures on different scales (from the apical surface of hepatocytes forming the BC to cells) and this may yield a more precise geometrical reconstruction in comparison with voxel-based methods (Figure 3A).
evidence: The authors suggest their method may be more accurate than alternatives with figure reference.

claim: The accuracy of both LDA and BNC approaches was comparable, reaching higher than 99% efficiency for hepatocyte recognition and about 92–95% for all cell types.
source: The accuracy of both approaches was comparable, reaching higher than 99% efficiency for hepatocyte recognition and about 92–95% for all cell types.
evidence: The authors report classification performance for both methods.

claim: Nuclear size and roundness were less informative than the parameters related to nuclear texture (e.g. moments of lacunarity) for cell type discrimination.
source: Although nuclear size and roundness were traditionally considered a priori as the most relevant parameters to discriminate hepatocytes from non-parenchymal cells (Baratta et al., 2009; O'Gorman et al., 1985), we found that they are less informative than the parameters related to nuclear texture (e.g. moments of lacunarity).
evidence: The authors report an unexpected finding about feature importance with citations.

claim: The analysis of parameters relevant for cell classification can shed light on the differences in cell morphology that are difficult to grasp by the naked eye.
source: The analysis of parameters relevant for cell classification can shed light on the differences in cell morphology that are difficult to grasp by the naked eye.
evidence: The authors discuss the value of computational analysis.

claim: The accurate active mesh-based cell shape estimation led to well-separated peaks of cell volume distribution, which failed to be discriminated by approximation through Voronoi tessellation.
source: The accurate active mesh-based cell shape estimation led to well-separated peaks of cell volume distribution (Figure 4A–C), which failed to be discriminated by approximation through Voronoi tessellation (Bock et al., 2010) (data not shown).
evidence: The authors compare their method to an alternative approach with citation and figure reference.

claim: Hepatocytes are heterogeneous in size, number of nuclei (mono and bi-nucleated cells) and DNA content (polyploidy).
source: It is well established that hepatocytes are heterogeneous in size, number of nuclei (mono and bi-nucleated cells) and DNA content (polyploidy).
evidence: The authors state established knowledge about hepatocyte heterogeneity.

claim: These features (size, nuclei number, DNA content) are not randomly distributed but follow a specific zonation pattern within the liver lobule.
source: However, we observed that these features are not randomly distributed but follow a specific zonation pattern within the liver lobule.
evidence: The authors report a novel finding about spatial organization.

claim: The spatial distribution of hepatocytes according to their ploidy in the CV-PV axes correlates with the metabolic zonation.
source: The spatial distribution of hepatocytes according to their ploidy in the CV-PV axes correlates with the metabolic zonation.
evidence: The authors identify a correlation between their findings and known metabolic zonation.

claim: This correlation suggests a possible role of polyploidy in regulating hepatocyte functions in the liver lobule.
source: This correlation suggests a possible role of polyploidy in regulating hepatocyte functions in the liver lobule.
evidence: The authors propose a hypothesis based on their findings.

claim: Two unique populations of cells with stem cell-like properties and the capacity to repopulate the liver have been recently identified.
source: Interestingly, two unique populations of cells with stem cell-like properties and the capacity to repopulate the liver have been recently identified (Ray, 2015; Wang et al., 2015; Font-Burgada et al., 2015).
evidence: The authors cite recent literature on liver stem cells.

claim: One population located close to the CV, which has been implicated in homeostatic hepatocyte renewal, coincides with the mono-nucleated 2n cells identified by the authors.
source: One population located close to the CV, which has been implicated in homeostatic hepatocyte renewal (Wang et al., 2015), coincides with the mono-nucleated 2n cells we identified.
evidence: The authors connect their findings to recent literature with citation.

claim: The other population of hepatocytes located near the PV, which was found to repopulate the liver after injury, could correspond to the low ploidy cells (2n and 2×2n) observed by the authors.
source: The other population of hepatocytes located near the PV, which was found to repopulate the liver after injury (Font-Burgada et al., 2015), could correspond to the low ploidy cells (2n and 2×2n) we observed.
evidence: The authors connect their findings to recent literature with citation.

claim: These results inspire future studies aimed at exploring the mechanisms underlying regulation of mono- versus bi-nuclearity and polyploidy in the context of liver tissue structure, function and regeneration.
source: These results inspire future studies aimed at exploring the mechanisms underlying regulation of mono- versus bi-nuclearity and polyploidy in the context of liver tissue structure, function and regeneration (Zaret, 2015; Ray, 2015).
evidence: The authors discuss implications for future research with citations.

claim: The accurate digital geometrical model of tissue is a valuable resource.
source: In this context, the accurate digital geometrical model of tissue is a valuable resource.
evidence: The authors state the value of their work.

claim: Geometrical models provide the means of extracting structural information as a precondition for the development of functional models of tissues.
source: Geometrical models provide the means of extracting structural information as a precondition for the development of functional models of tissues.
evidence: The authors state the importance of geometrical models for functional modeling.

claim: Geometrical models can be a tool for acquiring accurate quantitative measurements of morphological features and have the potential of uncovering the fundamental rules underlying tissue organization.
source: They can be a tool for acquiring accurate quantitative measurements of morphological features and, as such, have the potential of uncovering the fundamental rules underlying tissue organization.
evidence: The authors discuss the potential of geometrical models.

claim: The measurement of specific parameters, such as BC and sinusoid diameters, network cardinality, cell volume and shape, can serve as diagnostic markers of early stages of tissue dysfunction/repairing, thus providing new tools for clinical research and drug development.
source: In addition, the measurement of specific parameters, such as BC and sinusoid diameters, network cardinality, cell volume and shape, etc., can serve as diagnostic markers of early stages of tissue dysfunction/repairing, thus providing new tools for clinical research and drug development.
evidence: The authors discuss potential clinical applications of their work.

claim: Six- to nine-week-old C57BL/6JOlaHsd mice were purchased from Charles River Laboratory.
source: Six- to nine-week-old C57BL/6JOlaHsd mice were purchased from Charles River Laboratory.
evidence: The authors provide details about their experimental animals.

claim: All animal studies were conducted in accordance with German animal welfare legislation and in strict pathogen-free conditions in the animal facility of the Max Planck Institute of Molecular Cell Biology and Genetics, Dresden, Germany.
source: All animal studies were conducted in accordance with German animal welfare legislation and in strict pathogen-free conditions in the animal facility of the Max Planck Institute of Molecular Cell Biology and Genetics, Dresden, Germany.
